power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p-value < 0.05", "p-value < 0.05", 
"p-value < 0.05"), Text = c("To investigate whether variation in neuronal SEC61G expression statistically mediated the corresponding microglial trans associations, we applied structural equation model 53 (SEM) separately for each colocalized microglial trans-eGene and trans-eProgram (Methods). 10 gene-level and 2 program-level associations showed significant indirect effects (p-value < 0.05 based on donor bootstrap analysis) (Figures 5b).", 
"Among the ten proximal cis-eGenes, INO80E expression in excitatory neurons and oligodendrocytes showed nominally significant indirect associations with distal ABCA1 expression (p-value < 0.05; Figure 7f).", 
"These models yielded 14 and 15 indirect associations, respectively (p-value < 0.05; Supplementary Figures 14b-c)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 2 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **10 scripts need a person** to choose a file, answer a question or use an app, which cannot be reproduced without one: 3_cal_power_qvalue.R, 3_cal_power.R, 4_4_plt_power_low_caus_high_b.R, trans_pco_demo/script/p.R, plot.R, trans_pco_demo/script/prep.bed.R, trans_pco_demo/script/regress.out.covariates.R, signals.uniq.R, archie_p.R, archie_plot.R. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. **7 scripts stopped on a file another script writes**, so they were run once more after the other scripts: `5_significant_SNPs.R` (p.module_all.Sigma_nullz.rds); `6_1_combine_p.R` (p_all_1e5.rds); `6_2_significant_SNPs.R` (p_all_1e5.rds); `8_1_update_significant_SNPs_ratio_module_chr.R` (p_all_1e5.rds); `8_3_update_significant_SNPs_ratio.R` (p_all_1e5.rds); `dgn_w_cell_prop_pc.R` (p_all_1e5.rds); `4_2_plot_all_p.R` (p.module_all.Sigma_nullz.rds). 2 files were written in another folder than where the script looked, so before that run we copied them there: `output/p_all_1e5.rds` to `modules/FDR/p_all_1e5.rds` for `6_1_combine_p.R`; `eqtlgen/p/p.module_all.Sigma_nullz.rds` to `p/p.module_all.Sigma_nullz.rds` for `4_2_plot_all_p.R`. The scripts assume they all run from one folder; saying which, or building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), solves this. Then this one ran to the end: `6_1_combine_p.R`. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_).

text.text: Mapping genetic effects on distal genes and regulatory programs is essential for understanding how genetic variation influences complex diseases; yet trans-QTL discovery remains limited by weak effect sizes, extensive multiple testing and poor reproducibility.

Here, we introduce TransMap, a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale trans-QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants.

Beyond individual trans-eGenes, TransMap constructs local co-regulatory program phenotypes that account for background expression variation to improve the detection of weak, coordinated distal genetic effects.
Across a broad range of simulation settings, TransMap achieved 9.2-36.7% higher trans-QTL discovery power than existing methods while maintaining well-controlled type I error rates.

We applied TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles from the aging human brain in the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), further integrating proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic biomarker measurements (average N=476 donors).

Genome-wide fine-mapping of TransMap single-gene and program-level QTL yielded variant annotations with 2.75-2.88x heritability enrichment across 57 complex diseases and traits (average N=307K), with complementary heritability information captured across regulatory scales.

Multi-phenotype colocalization identified 49,532 trans-regulatory events supported by shared genetic signals with cis-eQTL or biomarker-QTL, including 1,825 candidate cis-trans-biomarker regulatory configurations.

TransMap further revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture in which neuronal cis-regulatory signals preferentially associate with coordinated glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomics.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized colocalization identified trans-regulatory associations in 115 AD-associated loci, including a KNOP1 cis-eQTL associated in trans with a microglial regulatory program containing MS4A4E, with additional support from statistical mediation analysis.
TransMap provides a multi-scale, cell-type-resolved atlas of trans-regulatory variation and a generalizable framework for elucidating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.

Most genetic variants associated with complex diseases lie in noncoding regions of the genome, yet the molecular mechanisms through which their effects propagate beyond proximal or cis-regulated genes to downstream cellular pathways remain incompletely understood [1] [2] [3] .
text.formatted: Most genetic variants associated with complex diseases lie in noncoding regions of the genome, yet the molecular mechanisms through which their effects propagate beyond proximal or cis-regulated genes to downstream cellular pathways remain incompletely understood <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> .

text.text: Trans-eQTL mapping, which identifies genetic variants associated with the expression of distant genes, provides a means to uncover regulatory networks and downstream molecular processes through which disease risk may propagate [4] [5] [6] .
text.formatted: Trans-eQTL mapping, which identifies genetic variants associated with the expression of distant genes, provides a means to uncover regulatory networks and downstream molecular processes through which disease risk may propagate <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> .

text.text: However, trans-eQTL discovery remains fundamentally challenging because individual distal effects are typically weak and the genome-wide variant-gene search space imposes a substantial multiple-testing burden 4, 7, 8 .
text.formatted: However, trans-eQTL discovery remains fundamentally challenging because individual distal effects are typically weak and the genome-wide variant-gene search space imposes a substantial multiple-testing burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: Large-scale studies such as eQTLGen 4, 9 and MetaBrain 10 have advanced trans-eQTL discovery through extensive sample aggregation, while more recent efforts including OneK1K 11 , SingleBrain 12 and PsychAD 13 have extended trans-eQTL mapping to individual cell types in immune cells and the human brain.

text.text: Nevertheless, detecting weak distal genetic effects remains particularly difficult at cell-type resolution, where molecular QTL cohorts typically have smaller effective sample sizes and greater measurement noise than large bulk-tissue studies 9 .
text.formatted: Nevertheless, detecting weak distal genetic effects remains particularly difficult at cell-type resolution, where molecular QTL cohorts typically have smaller effective sample sizes and greater measurement noise than large bulk-tissue studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: These challenges are particularly pronounced across many disease-relevant tissues where molecular QTL datasets remain comparatively limited in sample size, including GTEx tissues 7 , pancreatic islets 14 , and kidney cohorts 15 .

text.text: Recent methods, such as TransPCO 16 and ARCHIE 17 , have sought to improve sensitivity by aggregating coordinated distal genetic effects across multiple genes, but distinguishing subtle genetically coordinated regulatory programs from background expression variation remains challenging.

text.text: In parallel, the growing availability of molecular QTL maps across additional modalities, including large-scale proteomic and metabolomic resources, presents opportunities to leverage shared genetic signals across molecular phenotypes to strengthen transregulatory inference [18] [19] [20] [21] [22] .
text.formatted: In parallel, the growing availability of molecular QTL maps across additional modalities, including large-scale proteomic and metabolomic resources, presents opportunities to leverage shared genetic signals across molecular phenotypes to strengthen transregulatory inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> .

text.text: However, existing trans-QTL mapping approaches have not systematically combined gene-and program-level mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization across these molecular modalities.

Here, we introduce TransMap, a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale trans-QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants.
TransMap captures genetic regulation in a cell type at three complementary scales: individual distal genes, local co-regulatory programs and global genetically coordinated programs.

For local programs, TransMap uses background-whitened principal component analysis to capture coordinated regulatory variation while accounting for background expression covariance 23 , improving sensitivity to weak distal genetic effects.
text.formatted: For local programs, TransMap uses background-whitened principal component analysis to capture coordinated regulatory variation while accounting for background expression covariance <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> , improving sensitivity to weak distal genetic effects.

text.text: These complementary gene-and program-level representations are converted into quantitative molecular phenotypes for genome-wide QTL fine-mapping using SuSiE 24 .
text.formatted: These complementary gene-and program-level representations are converted into quantitative molecular phenotypes for genome-wide QTL fine-mapping using SuSiE <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> .

text.text: To further strengthen discovery, TransMap integrates cell-type resolved trans-eGene and trans-eProgram QTL with cell-type-resolved cis-eQTL and transacting biomarker-QTL through multi-phenotype colocalization using ColocBoost 25 .
text.formatted: To further strengthen discovery, TransMap integrates cell-type resolved trans-eGene and trans-eProgram QTL with cell-type-resolved cis-eQTL and transacting biomarker-QTL through multi-phenotype colocalization using ColocBoost <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: While program-level phenotypes improve the detection of coordinated distal genetic effects, multi-phenotype colocalization leverages shared genetic signals across molecular layers to support weaker trans-QTL associations that may not reach conventional single-phenotype significance thresholds.
Matching cis and trans signals across cell types can further nominate candidate cross-cell-type regulatory configurations and potential intercellular relationships for downstream investigation.

We applied TransMap to whole-genome genetic variation, bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles, and proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic measurements from the aging human brain in ROSMAP, as part of the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD) (N=361-784 donors; Supplementary Table 1), encompassing individual-gene expression phenotypes and transcriptomic program-level phenotypes across 6 cell types and 3 bulk regions [25] [26] [27] .
text.formatted: We applied TransMap to whole-genome genetic variation, bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles, and proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic measurements from the aging human brain in ROSMAP, as part of the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD) (N=361-784 donors; Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>), encompassing individual-gene expression phenotypes and transcriptomic program-level phenotypes across 6 cell types and 3 bulk regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref> .

text.text: TransMap was deployed in both disease-agnostic (xQTL-only) and Alzheimer's Disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized setting (GWAS-xQTL).
Gene programs from TransMap improved the detection of coordinated distal genetic effects relative to existing program-level approaches.
Across 57 relatively independent complex diseases and traits (average N=307K, genetic correlation 𝑟 !
< 0.7) 25 , TransMap eGene and eProgram QTL exhibited stronger disease heritability enrichment than existing methods and captured complementary genetic information across regulatory scales.

text.text: Multi-phenotype colocalization further identified trans-regulatory associations supported by shared genetic signals with proximal cis-eQTL and downstream biomarker-QTL, with program-level associations showing stronger concordance with biomarker QTL and functional gene networks.

These analyses also revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture, particularly linking neuronal cis-regulatory signals to glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by orthogonal co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomic analyses.
Finally, AD-centered colocalization identified candidate trans-regulatory associations at 115 AD-associated loci, connecting disease risk to distal genes, programs and molecular biomarkers.
These results establish TransMap as a generalizable framework and multiscale, cell-type-resolved resource for investigating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.
We present TransMap as an end-to-end framework for defining, genetically mapping and interpreting multi-scale trans-acting molecular phenotypes across diverse tissues and cell types (Figure 1a).
text.formatted: We present TransMap as an end-to-end framework for defining, genetically mapping and interpreting multi-scale trans-acting molecular phenotypes across diverse tissues and cell types (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: TransMap extends existing trans-QTL approaches along two major methodological dimensions: (i) from individual distal genes to quantitative phenotypes characterizing coordinated molecular responses within local and global gene programs, and (ii) from single-phenotype association testing to genome-wide multi-phenotype genetic colocalization across molecular modalities, leveraging additional molecular QTL maps, including cis-eQTL and biomarker-QTL when available, to strengthen the discovery and interpretation of distal genetic effects.
TransMap can be applied either in a disease-agnostic manner, with downstream applications across a broad range of complex diseases and traits, or in a disease-specific, GWAS-prioritized manner.
TransMap integrates whole-genome sequencing with donor-level, cell-type-resolved pseudobulk expression profiles to represent trans regulation at three complementary molecular scales.
At the individual-gene level, TransMap uses normalized expression of distal genes as the conventional unit of trans-eQTL analysis (Methods).
Additionally, TransMap defines compact local co-expression programs and broader global transregulatory programs.

At the local-program level, which we refer to as TransMap-local, TransMap identifies coexpression modules using Hotspot 28 and derives donor-level co-regulatory activity scores for each module using background-whitened principal component analysis (WPC) 23 (Methods).
text.formatted: At the local-program level, which we refer to as TransMap-local, TransMap identifies coexpression modules using Hotspot <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> and derives donor-level co-regulatory activity scores for each module using background-whitened principal component analysis (WPC) <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> (Methods).

text.text: Unlike conventional principal component analysis, which identifies dominant axes of expression variation, WPC prioritizes program-level variation relative to a background covariance structure, thereby reducing the influence of shared expression variation unrelated to the program.
For each gene program 𝒢, we first create 22 leave-one-chromosome-out (LOCO) programs, 𝒢 "# , by leaving out all genes from chromosome 𝑐.

WPC identifies a set of directions 𝑘 for the program 𝒢 "# by maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio of observed program-level variance to a size-matched background residual variance: where 𝚺 𝒢 "+ represents the expression covariance matrix corresponding to genes in 𝒢 "# , and 𝚺 * "+ represents the estimated background residual covariance matrix (Methods).
Let 𝑬 ∈ ℝ , × / denote the centered donor-by-gene expression matrix for 𝑛 individuals and 𝑞 genes, after removing relevant covariates.
The estimated WPC loading vectors 𝝎 & $,𝒢 "# are subsequently projected onto donor-level expression profiles to generate quantitative program activity phenotypes, 𝒀 $,𝒢 "# = 𝑬 𝒢 "# 𝝎 & $,𝒢 "# .

text.text: This procedure is repeated across all 22 autosomes to prevent the inclusion of genes located on the tested chromosome in the corresponding program phenotypes, thereby restricting the analysis to inter-chromosomal genetic effects.
This approach can also be generalized to pre-defined local gene programs (Methods).

At the global-program level, which we refer to as TransMap-global, TransMap captures genome-wide patterns of genetically coordinated expression by learning sparse variant and gene embeddings from inter-chromosomal variant-gene trans-associations using sparse canonical correlation analysis (sCCA) 29 (Methods).

text.text: The resulting gene embeddings are projected onto donor-level expression profiles in a LOCO manner to derive global program activity phenotypes.
TransMap also moves beyond trans-eQTL mapping of preselected variants to generate genome-wide, finemapped annotations of trans-regulatory potential.

For each individual-gene or program-level trans-acting phenotype (denoted by trans-eGene and trans-eProgram respectively), TransMap performs genome-wide finemapping using the SuSiE (Sum of Single Effects) 24 model across 1,361 approximately independent LD blocks 26 , yielding 95% credible sets (CS) and variant-level posterior inclusion probabilities (PIP) (Methods).

text.text: Unlike previous large-scale trans-eQTL studies, such as eQTLGen Phase II, which restricted fine-mapping to loci with significant associations 9 , TransMap performs genome-wide fine-mapping across individual-gene and programlevel phenotypes, retaining posterior evidence at loci that do not reach conventional association significance thresholds.

text.text: This strategy is motivated by recent studies demonstrating the utility of genome-wide fine-mapping for characterizing polygenic genetic architectures and informing downstream genetic analyses 30, 31 .

text.text: Additionally, we define genome-wide variant annotations using the maximum PIP (trans-MaxPIP) 32 across the corresponding trans phenotypes, constructing both cell-type-specific and cross-cell-type annotations.

text.text: We further perform joint heritability analyses of individual-gene and program-level trans-MaxPIP annotations, along with cis-eQTL-derived MaxPIP annotations, to assess whether distinct scales of distal regulation capture complementary disease-relevant genetic information beyond proximal cis-regulatory annotations.

Finally, TransMap leverages multi-phenotype genetic colocalization using ColocBoost 25 to integrate cell-typeresolved trans-eGene and trans-eProgram QTL with proximal cis-eQTL and additional biomarker-QTL, thereby improving both trans-QTL discovery and functional interpretation (Methods, Figure 1a).
text.formatted: Finally, TransMap leverages multi-phenotype genetic colocalization using ColocBoost <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> to integrate cell-typeresolved trans-eGene and trans-eProgram QTL with proximal cis-eQTL and additional biomarker-QTL, thereby improving both trans-QTL discovery and functional interpretation (Methods, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: Because proximal cis-eQTL and distal trans-QTL can differ substantially in effect size and statistical power, we perform separate genome-wide colocalization analyses: (i) gene-level cis-eQTL colocalization across cell types, and (ii) LD-blocklevel colocalization of trans-eGene, trans-eProgram and biomarker QTL across molecular phenotypes and cell types.
We subsequently integrate events from these analyses based on shared genetic signals.
Each colocalization event is characterized by this integrated colocalization confidence set (CoS) and an associated configuration of molecular phenotypes sharing the genetic signal.
ColocBoost also provides a variant-level colocalization probability (VCP) in alignment with the posterior inclusion probability (PIP) in standard finemapping (Methods).

This approach provides convergent genetic evidence for distal regulatory associations, including weak trans-QTL associations that may not achieve conventional single-phenotype significance thresholds.

In the FunGen-AD application, we integrate cell-type-resolved trans-QTL and cis-eQTL across 6 cell types and 3 bulk regions with molecular QTL for proteins, glycoproteins and metabolites measured in the aging human brain cortex 26, 27 .

text.text: Using shared distal genetic signals through genome-wide multi-phenotype colocalization, we nominate candidate cis-trans and cis-trans-biomarker regulatory configurations.

We define the cell types associated with proximal cis-regulated genes as the putative "initiating cell types" and those associated with distal trans-eGenes or trans-ePrograms as the putative "recipient cell types" (Figure 1a).
text.formatted: We define the cell types associated with proximal cis-regulated genes as the putative "initiating cell types" and those associated with distal trans-eGenes or trans-ePrograms as the putative "recipient cell types" (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: These designations describe the positions of cell types within candidate regulatory configurations rather than experimentally established directions of signaling.
This framework therefore enables the characterization of shared genetic associations across molecular layers and cellular contexts, extending conventional bulk cis-trans regulatory mapping.
However, colocalization does not establish that a cis-regulated gene causally mediates a distal effect or that associations across cell types reflect direct intercellular signaling.

Subsequent pathway-level, spatial and co-culture experimental analyses provide orthogonal evidence for the biological coherence, anatomical organization and cellular interaction signatures of the nominated configurations.

The AD GWASprioritized ColocBoost analysis further assesses whether disease-associated genetic signals are shared with proximal cis-eQTL, distal trans-QTL or biomarker-QTL, thereby nominating candidate genes, programs, molecular biomarkers and cellular contexts for downstream functional investigation of AD susceptibility loci.

The TransMap framework is implemented as a command-line interface with modular components for transphenotype construction, QTL fine-mapping, and multi-phenotype colocalization (see Code Availability).
Summary statistics from all program-level QTL maps and colocalization results are made publicly available to facilitate downstream analyses and broader scientific use (see Data Availability).

Having defined local and global program-level phenotypes, we first evaluated whether these representations capture coordinated distal genetic effects, using independent trans-eQTL resources and simulation benchmarks.
For local programs, we first asked whether Hotspot-derived co-expression modules grouped genes exhibiting shared trans-eQTL associations.

We quantified "trans-eQTL coherence" for each significant variant-program pair as the proportion of constituent genes exhibiting suggestive association with the same distal variant (individual-gene association p-value< 10 "0 ) (Methods).
text.formatted: We quantified "trans-eQTL coherence" for each significant variant-program pair as the proportion of constituent genes exhibiting suggestive association with the same distal variant (individual-gene association p-value< 10 "0 ) (Methods).

text.text: Higher coherence therefore indicates that a programlevel genetic association is supported by a larger fraction of its constituent genes, reflecting tighter coordination of distal genetic associations within the program.

Hotspot programs derived from GTEx brain cortex and whole blood expression data showed 1.6-fold and 1.8-fold higher mean trans-eQTL coherence compared to WGCNA programs when evaluated against independent MetaBrain and eQTLGen bulk trans-eQTL associations respectively (Figure 1b).

text.text: Among significant TransMap-eGene QTL associations, 19.9% involved genetic signals associated with multiple distal genes, compared with 10.5% of cis-eQTL associations involving multiple proximal genes.
Similarly, 26.4% of TransMap-local QTL associations involved multiple programs.

Given the large number of correlated molecular phenotypes and genome-wide genetic associations evaluated in trans-QTL mapping, we independently assessed the empirical calibration of the nominal FDR-controlled discoveries using genotypelabel permutations.

The empirical FDR ranged 4.8%-9.2% in bulk contexts and ranged 7.7% to 14.9% across six cell types (Supplementary Figure 3b), indicating that conventional significance thresholds did not uniformly achieve nominal FDR control for single-phenotype trans-QTL mapping.

text.text: These findings motivate the integration of complementary molecular-QTL evidence through multi-phenotype colocalization to provide additional statistical support for weak distal genetic associations, as evaluated in subsequent sections.

We generated 3 genome-wide variant-level trans-MaxPIP annotations separately for individual-gene (TransMap-eGene-MaxPIP), local-program (TransMap-local-MaxPIP) and global-program (TransMap-global-MaxPIP) phenotypes by aggregating fine-mapping posterior inclusion probabilities across phenotypes and cell types (Methods).

We evaluated their disease relevance using two S-LDSC metrics: heritability enrichment and standardized effect size (𝜏 ⋆ ), the latter quantifying annotation informativeness conditional on other annotations in the model.

In the meta-analysis across 57 traits, 2 out of 3 annotations (TransMap-eGene-MaxPIP and TransMap-local-MaxPIP) showed high heritability enrichment (2.75x-2.88x) (p-value ranging from 2.9 × 10 "23 to 4.3 × 10 "24 ) and 𝜏 ⋆ (0.22-0.27) (p-value ranging from 6.5 × 10 "56 to 3.5 × 10 "55 ) conditional on the baseline annotations (Figure 2c).

text.text: These results indicate that individual distal genes and compact local programs capture complementary components of complex-trait genetic architecture, whereas broad global programs contribute no detectable heritability beyond baseline annotations.
We next benchmarked the disease relevance of TransMap annotations against existing approaches.
At the local program scale, we compared TransMap-local-MaxPIP annotation against analogous trans-MaxPIP annotations generated using Eigengene, TransPCO and AUCell approaches (Methods).

Because TransPCO combines multiple principal components (PC)-level association statistics using an ACAT omnibus test, we adapted it for fine-mapping by separately fine-mapping retained PCs and aggregating their PIPs into a MaxPIP annotation (TransPCO*-MaxPIP; Methods).

text.text: We conclude that genome-wide trans-QTL fine-mapping yields reproducible and disease-informative variant annotations, with individual distal genes and compact local programs capturing complementary components of complex-trait genetic architecture.

Having established the disease relevance of individual-gene and local-program trans-QTL annotations, we next investigated whether distal genetic associations could be linked to proximal gene regulation and downstream bulk-level biomarker molecular phenotypes (proteins, glycoproteins and metabolites) through shared genetic signals.

We performed a genome-wide multi-phenotype colocalization using ColocBoost 25 (Methods), representing each shared causal variant by a colocalization confidence set (CoS) if it contained at least one variant at p-value<10 "0 and its associated configuration of molecular phenotypes sharing the genetic signal.

text.text: We next examined the functional properties of genes associated with these colocalization events.
We classified the colocalization events as cis-only, cis-trans or trans-only based on the representation of cis and trans phenotypes among colocalized phenotypes (Methods).

Pairs of distal trans-eGenes implicated by the same colocalization event showed 1.5-fold enrichment (p-value=0.009) for known protein-protein interactions in the STRING database 45 , whereas pairs connecting proximal cis-eGenes and distal trans-eGenes showed no detectable enrichment (Figure 3f).

text.text: Importantly, pairs of highly weighted genes within the same program exhibited an even higher 1.86-fold enrichment in protein-protein interactions.
These results indicate that program-level trans-QTL preferentially implicate groups of functionally connected genes, complementing their stronger convergence with biomarker-QTL.
We further examined whether cis-only, cis-trans and trans-only colocalization events exhibited distinct genomic and evolutionary properties.

This observation is consistent with recent reports that trans-regulatory loci can occur near highly constrained genes 46 , although the functional relationship between these genes and the associated distal molecular phenotypes remains unresolved.

text.text: Overall, these analyses establish that multi-phenotype colocalization provides additional statistical support for distal genetic associations and reveals complementary molecular and functional properties of individual-gene and program-level trans-QTL.

In particular, local-program associations show stronger convergence with biomarker variation and functionally connected gene networks, supporting their utility for interpreting distal regulatory effects across molecular layers.

TransMap provides a generalizable framework for performing (i) multiscale cell-type-resolved trans-QTL mapping, involving individual genes and gene programs, and (ii) multi-phenotype colocalization of these trans-QTL with cell-type-resolved cis-eQTL and biomarker-QTL.

Applied to the aging human brain through the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), TransMap provides a cell-type-resolved atlas of transregulatory variation and their relationships with AD-associated genetic variation.

The resulting maps reveal (i) complementary contributions of individual-gene and local program-level QTL annotations to complex trait heritability, (ii) stronger correspondence of program-level genetic signals with downstream biomarker-QTL and functional networks, (iii) candidate cis-trans regulatory configurations spanning distinct brain cell types, and (iv) expanded interpretation of AD susceptibility loci through shared genetic associations with distal genes, regulatory programs and molecular biomarkers.

A central insight from TransMap is that distal genetic regulation can be more sensitively detected and functionally characterized through coordinated molecular responses than through individual gene associations alone.

Although a regulatory variant may exert only weak effects on individual distal genes, its effects can converge on groups of co-regulated genes, producing a more detectable program-level genetic signal.

TransMap's whitened PCA approach improves the detection of coordinated trans effects while accounting for background expression covariance and capturing multiple axes of regulatory variation within a program.

Notably, individual-gene and local-program trans-QTL annotations capture complementary components of complex-trait heritability despite being derived from the same transcriptomic measurements, highlighting the value of representing distal genetic regulation at multiple molecular scales.

Complementing this program-based strategy, multi-phenotype colocalization leverages shared genetic signals across molecular phenotypes to support weak trans associations that may not achieve conventional significance thresholds individually.

More broadly, the integration of multiple molecular modalities provides complementary views of the consequences of genetic variation, allowing evidence from proximal gene regulation, distal expression programs and molecular biomarkers to jointly inform transregulatory inference.

By connecting these complementary molecular phenotypes through shared genetic signals, TransMap can pinpoint candidate regulatory relationships underlying an association, providing a more detailed basis for downstream functional investigation.

The stronger convergence of program-level trans-QTL with biomarker-QTL and functional protein networks further suggests that coordinated expression programs provide informative representations of distal genetic effects across molecular layers.

Moreover, the enrichment of neuronal cis-regulatory signals among loci associated with glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by coculture and spatial transcriptomic analyses, suggests that distal genetic regulation may involve relationships across cellular contexts rather than being restricted to the cell type containing the proximal genetic effect.

This has broader implications for disease-variant interpretation, as the cellular context of proximal gene regulation may differ from those exhibiting associated distal molecular responses, as also highlighted in recent mouse models 72, 73 .
text.formatted: This has broader implications for disease-variant interpretation, as the cellular context of proximal gene regulation may differ from those exhibiting associated distal molecular responses, as also highlighted in recent mouse models <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">72,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">73</ref> .

text.text: These findings support a multiscale and multimodal view of trans regulation in which genetic effects are distributed across coordinated molecular programs, molecular layers and cellular contexts.
TransMap provides several reusable outputs and opportunities for downstream applications in human genetics.

First, its modular end-to-end pipeline for trans-acting phenotype construction, genome-wide QTL fine-mapping, and multi-phenotype colocalization, can be deployed across diverse tissues, cell types and molecular QTL cohorts.
This framework may be particularly useful in tissue-specific or cell-type-resolved QTL datasets with modest sample sizes, where conventional individual-gene trans-QTL discovery remains underpowered.

Moreover, as molecular QTL resources expand across transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and other molecular measurements, integrating these complementary genetic views offers opportunities to improve the detection and functional interpretation of distal regulatory effects.

Second, although the gene programs examined in this study were primarily derived from the analyzed tissues, TransMap can also incorporate externally defined gene programs, including those identified from mouse models or genetic perturbation experiments, to investigate their regulation by human genetic variation.

Third, genome-wide fine-mapped trans-eGene and trans-eProgram QTL provide variant-level annotations that can complement cis-eQTL annotations in functional annotation-based heritability analyses 32, 34 and potentially inform polygenic risk prediction 74, 75 and polygenic localization methods 30 across a broad range of complex diseases and traits.

text.text: Fourth, cis-regulated genes and distal trans-eGenes or trans-ePrograms implicated through colocalization with disease GWAS provide specific molecular and cellular hypotheses for targeted functional validation.

In particular, cell-type-resolved cis-trans regulatory configurations can guide the design of cell-type-specific CRISPR perturbation experiments in co-culture systems, where candidate cis-regulated genes are perturbed in putative initiating cell types and their predicted distal transcriptional responses are measured in recipient cell types 76 .

text.text: Finally, while the present study primarily focuses on molecular assays with single readouts, we are currently extending TransMap to 10X scRNA+ATAC multiome datasets as part of the FunGen-AD effort to characterize distal genetic regulation across coupled molecular layers.
Our work has several limitations, representing important directions for future research.

First, the substantial differences in effect sizes between proximal cis-eQTL and weaker distal trans-QTL create statistical challenges for performing untargeted multi-phenotype colocalization jointly across cis and trans phenotypes, motivating our strategy of performing separate cis-and trans-QTL colocalization analyses, followed by integration of colocalization events sharing genetic signals.
Additionally, weak individual-gene cell-type-resolved trans-QTL associations exhibited elevated empirical false discovery rates despite nominal FDR control.

In contrast, multiphenotype colocalization yielded trans-regulatory associations with lower empirical false discovery rates in the evaluated permutation analyses and stronger concordance with independent trans-QTL resources (Supplementary Figure 4c).
text.formatted: In contrast, multiphenotype colocalization yielded trans-regulatory associations with lower empirical false discovery rates in the evaluated permutation analyses and stronger concordance with independent trans-QTL resources (Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4c</ref>).

text.text: Further methodological development is needed to accommodate differences in statistical power across molecular phenotypes and enable more comprehensive joint cis-trans colocalization.

Second, although TransMap identifies candidate configurations through multi-phenotype colocalization, shared genetic associations do not establish that a cis-regulated gene causally mediates a downstream trans effect or that cross-cell-type associations reflect direct intercellular signaling.

Although statistical mediation, co-culture and spatial transcriptomic analyses provide complementary support for selected configurations, targeted genetic perturbation experiments will be important for establishing the causal architecture of these regulatory relationships.
Third, the performance of background-whitened PCA depends on accurately estimating the background expression covariance structure.
Limited sample sizes, expression sparsity and heterogeneous cellular states may compromise this estimation and affect the sensitivity and interpretability of derived programs.
Fourth, strong residual correlations among molecular phenotypes can result in loss of power for large-scale multiphenotype colocalization, as highlighted in the ColocBoost paper 25 .

text.text: The residual correlations estimated in the present datasets fall within the range where statistical power and false discovery rates were generally well maintained 25 , and empirical permutation analyses further support favorable null calibration in the current application.

text.text: Fifth, the present study does not systematically address cross-cohort harmonization of expression measurements, program definitions and genetic association signals, which will be necessary for integrating independently generated trans-QTL maps and improving portability across datasets and populations.

TransMap is proposed as an end-to-end computational framework that represents trans regulation at three molecular resolutions from gene expression, including individual distal genes (trans-eGene) and gene programs (trans-eProgram).
A gene program may be represented by a set of small number of genes (typically ranging from tens to hundreds of genes) or a continuous weighting of all genes genome-wide (Figure 1a).

These cell-type resolved trans-QTL are then analyzed together with cell-type-resolved cis-eQTL and downstream bulk tissue biomarker-QTL using multi-phenotype colocalization, which tests whether proximal cis signals, distal trans signals and downstream biomarker signals are consistent with a shared underlying genetic locus.
Colocalization indicates compatibility with a shared causal variant across a set of molecular phenotypes but does not establish mediation or direct intercellular signaling.

text.text: Because correlation among phenotypes does not alter the expected number of false positives, these estimates are approximately unbiased but do not account for residual p-value miscalibration, which we assess empirically using genotype-label permutations.
To enable program-level QTL discovery beyond co-expression modules, we extended TransMap to analyze any prespecified functional gene set.
For each gene set and expression context, TransMap applies the WPC procedure used for TransMap-local to derive donor-level co-regulatory activity scores.
Each retained WPC is treated as a quantitative molecular phenotype and subjected to genome-wide fine-mapping across 1,361 LD blocks 26 .
text.formatted: Each retained WPC is treated as a quantitative molecular phenotype and subjected to genome-wide fine-mapping across 1,361 LD blocks <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: For trans-specific mapping of variants on chromosome 𝑐, genes located on this chromosome are excluded before phenotype construction; complementary network-wide mapping retain all member genes to capture genetic effects on the complete program.

To evaluate curated biological programs, we analyzed the 50 Hallmark gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) previously examined using TransPCO 16 , comprising 32-200 genes and provide coherent and relatively nonredundant representation of biological states and processes.
text.formatted: To evaluate curated biological programs, we analyzed the 50 Hallmark gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) previously examined using TransPCO <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> , comprising 32-200 genes and provide coherent and relatively nonredundant representation of biological states and processes.

text.text: To evaluate data-driven regulatory programs, we inferred context-specific TF-target regulons separately for six major brain cell types and three bulk cortical regions using SCENIC 44 : GRNBoost2 78 was first used to estimate weighted regulatory association between human TFs and all expressed genes, after which the top highest-ranked targets per TF were partitioned according to their correlation direction and pruned using RcisTarge motif enrichment (normalized enrichment score > 3.0) 79 .
text.formatted: To evaluate data-driven regulatory programs, we inferred context-specific TF-target regulons separately for six major brain cell types and three bulk cortical regions using SCENIC 44 : GRNBoost2 <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">78</ref> was first used to estimate weighted regulatory association between human TFs and all expressed genes, after which the top highest-ranked targets per TF were partitioned according to their correlation direction and pruned using RcisTarge motif enrichment (normalized enrichment score > 3.0) <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">79</ref> .

text.text: The resulting motif-supported regulons and Hallmark gene sets were summarized using WPC and mapped using the same genome-wide framework.
These applications establish TransMap as a general-purpose for converting curated or data-driven gene sets into quantitative phenotype for program-level QTL discovery.
A trans-QTL can represent a downstream molecular consequence of a proximal cis effect, in which local genetic regulation propagates to distal molecular phenotypes within or across cell types.
These effects may further converge with downstream biomarker signals measured through proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic assays.
Proximal cis-regulatory genes are relatively few and typically have stronger cis-QTL effects, whereas distal trans-regulatory phenotypes are far more numerous and individually weaker 7 .
text.formatted: Proximal cis-regulatory genes are relatively few and typically have stronger cis-QTL effects, whereas distal trans-regulatory phenotypes are far more numerous and individually weaker <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: This imbalance in dimensionality and association strength can substantially limit power for a single joint colocalization analysis.
We therefore implemented a two-stage genome-wide multi-phenotype colocalization strategy using ColocBoost 25.
text.formatted: We therefore implemented a two-stage genome-wide multi-phenotype colocalization strategy using ColocBoost <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref>.

text.text: In the first stage, we identified colocalization among distal molecular phenotypes within the same 1,361 extended LD block regions.
Candidate phenotypes comprised cell-type-resolved trans genes and trans programs together with trans biomarkers when available.
Within each region, we retained phenotypes for which fine-mapping identified at least one 50% CS overlapping the region 26 .
text.formatted: Within each region, we retained phenotypes for which fine-mapping identified at least one 50% CS overlapping the region <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: To reduce redundancy, highly correlated phenotypes were pruned within each phenotype class at an absolute pairwise correlation of | 𝑟 |≥ 0.7.
ColocBoost was then applied jointly to the retained distal phenotypes.

Each trans-only colocalization event was summarized by a 95% colocalization confidence set (CoS), variant-level variant colocalization probabilities (VCP), and a trait configuration specifying the subset of phenotypes compatible with the shared genetic signal.
We retained 95% CoS as an independent locus for colocalization events when it contains at least one variant with marginal pvalue < 10 "0 for the traits in configurations.
text.formatted: We retained 95% CoS as an independent locus for colocalization events when it contains at least one variant with marginal pvalue < 10 "0 for the traits in configurations.

text.text: In the second stage, we matched these distal colocalization events to events from a separate genome-wide gene-level colocalization analysis of cell-type-resolved cis-eQTL 26 .
text.formatted: In the second stage, we matched these distal colocalization events to events from a separate genome-wide gene-level colocalization analysis of cell-type-resolved cis-eQTL <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: A distal trans-only colocalization event and a proximal cis-only colocalization event were integrated when their 95% CoS shared the same causal variants.
Therefore, we define a `Colocalization Event` as this integrated colocalization confidence set and an associated configuration of molecular phenotypes sharing the genetic signal.

Configurations that link one or more proximal cis-eGenes to one or more distal trans-eGenes or trans-ePrograms were defined as `Candidate Regulatory Configurations`, indicating the core cis-trans link and may further connect to a downstream trans-biomarker.
The cis-effect cell types define 'initiating cell types', whereas the distal trans-effect cell types define 'recipient cell types' (Figure 1a).
text.formatted: The cis-effect cell types define 'initiating cell types', whereas the distal trans-effect cell types define 'recipient cell types' (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: Because the two stages were connected through overlap between independently estimated colocalization events, these configurations do not represent formal joint cis-trans colocalization and cannot establish mediation or direct intercellular signaling.
Nevertheless, this design allows TransMap to organize shared regulatory evidence across molecular scales and cell types for subsequent biological characterization.

In contrast to LD-block-based genome-wide fine-mapping and colocalization analyses, AD-prioritized colocalization was organized around topologically associating domain (TAD)-based regions containing candidate AD loci.
We extracted candidate AD loci curated by the FunGen-xQTL project 26 and mapped their constituent variants by genomic position to a genome-wide reference set of 1,328 TAD regions 27 .
text.formatted: We extracted candidate AD loci curated by the FunGen-xQTL project <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> and mapped their constituent variants by genomic position to a genome-wide reference set of 1,328 TAD regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> .

text.text: Regions containing at least one candidate AD variant were retained, and candidate variants mapping to the same TAD region were analyzed jointly.

Because a TAD region may contain multiple proximal genes, each TAD region was therefore extended to encompass the cis windows of all candidate genes assigned to that region, with each window defined as ±1.5 Mb from the transcription start site 27.
text.formatted: Because a TAD region may contain multiple proximal genes, each TAD region was therefore extended to encompass the cis windows of all candidate genes assigned to that region, with each window defined as ±1.5 Mb from the transcription start site <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref>.

text.text: For each tested TAD region on chromosome 𝑐, we performed targeted QTL mapping of all candidate molecular phenotypes at the AD variants assigned to this region.

Candidate proximal phenotypes comprised cell-typesolved expression traits for genes within the TAD region; candidate distal phenotypes comprised cell-typeresolved TransMap phenotypes constructed from genes outside chromosome 𝑐.
Proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic phenotypes were additionally evaluated as potential downstream trans-biomarkers.

A molecular phenotype was retained for colocalization analysis if at least one candidate AD variant in this TAD region showed a marginal QTL association at p-value< 10 "8 as suggested in ColocBoost 25 .
text.formatted: A molecular phenotype was retained for colocalization analysis if at least one candidate AD variant in this TAD region showed a marginal QTL association at p-value< 10 "8 as suggested in ColocBoost <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: We jointly analyzed all retained molecular phenotypes with an AD GWAS meta-analysis using the disease-prioritized mode of ColocBoost in each TAD region, with AD designed as the focal trait (Data resources and preprocessing below).
This mode uses expedited single-effect coupling to prioritize colocalization signals involving AD while allowing multiple distinct signals within the region.
Each colocalization event was summarized by a 95% CoS, where its corresponding trait configuration specified the molecular phenotypes sharing the AD-associated signal.

We retained colocalization events linking AD to at least one molecular phenotype and containing at least one variant with marginal p-value < 10 "8 for AD colocalized molecular traits in configuration 25 .
text.formatted: We retained colocalization events linking AD to at least one molecular phenotype and containing at least one variant with marginal p-value < 10 "8 for AD colocalized molecular traits in configuration <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> .

text.text: We then classified retained colocalization events as AD-cis, AD-trans or AD-cis-trans according to whether the configuration contained proximal cis-eGenes, distal trans phenotypes or both.
AD-cis-trans configurations were interpreted as ADsupported candidate cis-trans regulatory paths.

For comparison, we additionally fine-mapped the AD GWAS using SuSiE and classified an AD locus as AD-only when its 95% CS shared no variants with any AD-centered 95% CoS containing at least one molecular effect.

To assess the calibration and robustness of TransMap, we performed two complementary empirical analyses: (i) 50:50 split-sample analyses to assess reproducibility of trans-MaxPIP annotation from genome-wide finemapping analysis, and (ii) genome-wide permutation analyses to evaluate the null calibration of fine-mapping and multi-phenotype colocalization for downstream trans-QTL discovery.

These analyses evaluated two distinct properties of the framework: control of spurious discoveries under the null and generalizability of the inferred programs and genetic associations across donor subsets.
(i) Split-sample assessment of TransMap trans-MaxPIP annotation reproducibility.
We randomly divided donors into two non-overlapping halves (50:50 donor-level split) for each expression profile.
We ran the full workflow independently in each split, including trans phenotype construction and genome-wide fine-mapping at three trans-regulatory scales.

Thus, Hotspot modules, WPC co-regulatory activity phenotypes and sCCA-derived global embeddings were estimated independently in the two splits, without transferring program definitions or model parameters between two splits.
We evaluated reproducibility using two complementary metrics.
First, we calculate the Pearson correlation between split-specific trans-MaxPIP annotations, separately for three transregulatory scales.
Second, we evaluated whether the independently derived annotations captured consistent disease-relevance genetic information.
We applied the same S-LDSC models to each split-specific trans-MaxPIP annotation and compared heritability enrichment and marginal 𝜏 * estimates (Methods below).
(ii) Permutation-based assessment of null calibration.

We assessed the calibration of fine-mapping using SuSiE for individual trans genes and multi-phenotype colocalization using ColocBoost when jointly analyzing thousands of trans-eGene, trans-eProgram, and trans-biomarker phenotypes.
We performed genome-wide permutations across 1,361 LD blocks used in the primary analyses.

For statistical fine-mapping, we randomly shuffled donor labels in the genotype matrix while molecular phenotypes was unchanged; then we applied SuSiE to each permuted block and defined the genome-wide empirical false discovery rate (FDR) as the number of fine-mapped trans-eQTL under permutation divided by the number of trans-eQTL detected in the original data.
For multiphenotype colocalization, two permutation schemes separated the effect of analyzing thousands of phenotypes from that of their observed correlation structure.

First, to assess null colocalization events when cross-phenotype correlations were disrupted, we independently permuted donor labels for each trans-phenotype within each block while leaving the genotype matrix unchanged.
This preserved LD among variants but disrupted genotypephenotype associations and the observed correlations among trans-phenotypes.

Second, to assess null colocalization events under the phenotype covariance present in the primary analysis, we applied a single donorlabel permutation to the genotype matrix within each block while leaving all trans-phenotypes unchanged.
This procedure preserved both LD among variants and covariance among trans-phenotypes while disrupting genotype-phenotype associations.

We reran ColocBoost under each permutation scheme and estimated a genome-wide empirical FDR as the number of colocalization events detected under permutation divided by the number of events detected in the original data.
To account for differences in the number of phenotypes tested across LD blocks, we also calculated a weighted FDR.
Each detected event was weighted by the fraction of phenotype in its trait configuration among all phenotypes tested in that block, with identical weights applied to permuted and observed events.
We then matched this permuted trans-only colocalization events to genome-wide cis-gene events identified from the unpermuted data.
A false cis-trans match required at least one shared variant between their 95% CoS.
The genome-wide empirical cis-trans FDR was calculated as the number of cistrans matches obtained under permutation divided by the number of cis-trans matches obtained in the original analysis.

The primary molecular resources included bulk and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles across 6 cell types and 3 brain regions, and bulk proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic measurements from the aging brain cortex.
Bulk RNA-seq data were generated from postmortem tissues including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and anterior cingulate cortex (AC).
Standard QC and adapter trimming was performed on raw reads, followed by alignment via STAR and gene expression quantification via RNASeqQC 82, 83 .

text.text: For TransMap-local, we benchmarked two complementary components: the regulatory coherence of local coexpression modules and its utility for trans-QTL mapping.
First, using independent empirical trans-eQTL datasets, we tested whether the co-expression modules defining local programs grouped genes with coordinated trans-regulatory effects.
We used empirical evidence because simulations do not readily capture the complex covariance structure of gene expression in human tissues.
Second, we used simulations to assess whether WPC-based program phenotypes improved trans-QTL detection for a specified local program.
We first benchmarked Hotspot against WGCNA, a widely used method for detecting co-expression modules, using external and internal trans-eQTL resources.
Hotspot and WGCNA modules were constructed from the same donor-level expression resource, with method-specific parameters described in Methods.
Variant-program pairs were considered active when the program-level association passed the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of 10 "0 .

Larger coherence indicates that a program-level association is supported by multiple genes in the module rather than by a single outlier gene.

text.text: We used two principal metrics: statistical power and T1E.
Power was defined as the proportion of true module-level trans-QTL correctly identified across replicates, and T1E was defined as the proportion of null replicates in which a trans-QTL was detected.
For each simulation setting, 1,000 replicates were generated to evaluate statistical power and 10 6 replicates were generated to evaluate T1E at nominal pvalue of 10 "0.
For TransMap-global, we benchmarked whether sparse association-driven embeddings recovered the underlying variant-gene trans-effect structure.

Unlike the local benchmark, which evaluates trans-QTL detection for a specified gene module, the global benchmark evaluates recovery of low-dimensional regulatory structure at the variant-gene pair level.

We used a structured causal-network simulation following the benchmark developed for ARCHIE 17 , in which groups of variants act through upstream regulated genes and induce coordinated but indirect distal expression responses.

In this structured network, trans-active variants are organized into five-SNP blocks, and each block affects the expression of one proximal cis-gene mediator.
The proximal mediators then propagate effects through three downstream trans-gene layers (Figure 1f).

text.text: The primary numerical study considered four broad settings: (i) trans heritability, varied by changing the downstream layer-specific effect sizes to span low-(0.0025), intermediate-(0.004) and high-power (0.01) regimes for the weakest layer, and (ii) embedding sparsity, varied by changing the target proportion of non-zero loadings under sparse (0.4), dense (0.8) and cross-validation-optimized settings.
We additionally generated an independent held-out sample of 1,000 individuals for methods requiring an expression covariance estimate.

Details of the competing-method implementation are provided in Methods.
Performance was evaluated at the level of variant-gene trans-effect recovery from paired variant and gene embeddings using precision-recall curves (PRC).

PRC was obtained by ranking variant-gene pairs according to 𝑆 M! , with true positives defined as simulated trans variant-gene pairs connected by a non-zero directed path from a variant to a distal gene.
Precision was defined as the proportion of selected pairs in true trans variant-gene pairs, recall was defined as the proportion of true pairs recovered.
In simulations, we compared TransMap-local with conventional single-gene trans-eQTL testing (trans-eGene) and two local program-level trans-QTL calling methods, Eigengene 40 and TransPCO 16 .

text.text: For a module containing 𝑀 genes, trans-eGene tested each gene separately and assigned the module a Bonferroni-corrected p-value.
For Eigengene, we computed the first principal component (PC) of the donor-level expression matrix using `prcomp` in R and tested its association with each variant by linear regression.
We ran TransPCO using the code provided in https://github.com/liliw-w/Trans which retained components with eigenvalues 𝜆 > 0.1 and combined the six PC-based association test p-values by ACAT 88, 89 .

For the real data heritability comparisons, we converted competing methods into donor-level phenotypes wherever the original method did not provide phenotypes suitable for statistical fine-mapping analysis.
Eigengene was fine-mapped using the same chromosome-exclusion strategy to construct phenotype from the first PC of the donor-level expression matrix.

Because the native TransPCO test produces a variant-level combined p-value rather than a program activity phenotype, we defined TransPCO* by retaining expression PCs with eigenvalues 𝜆 > 0.1 and fine-mapping each PC separately; TransPCO* is therefore an adaptation for finemapping, not the original ACAT test by combining p-values from six PC-based association tests.
